summary:
The Lineweaver–Burk plot linearises Michaelis–Menten kinetics: 1/v against 1/[S] gives a straight line whose intercepts are 1/Vmax and −1/Km. It returns vmax, km and vmax/Km, and the panel shows all of them at once.

Enter two substrate/velocity pairs and the calculator returns Vmax, Km and catalytic efficiency. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lineweaver-Burk Plot / Km & Vmax
sections.html:
1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
*S*substrate concentrationmM
vinitial velocityµmol/min
Vmaxvelocity at saturating substrateµmol/min
Kmsubstrate concentration at half VmaxmM

Where the relationship comes from. Lineweaver & Burk (1934); the cautions on the double-reciprocal fit follow Dowd & Riggs (1965).

sections.title: How do I use the Lineweaver-Burk Plot / Km & Vmax?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: substrate concentration 1 of 0.5 mM, initial velocity 1 of 0.35 µmol/min, substrate concentration 2 of 2 mM, initial velocity 2 of 0.62 µmol/min.

Substituting them into the formula gives vmax of 0.8346 µmol/min, km of 0.6923 mM, vmax/km of 1.21 µmol/min/mM.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• With two points, Vmax and Km are exact for a linear fit but very sensitive to a single bad measurement; four to six points from 0.2 to 5 × Km is the practical minimum.

  • The double-reciprocal plot weights the lowest substrate points most heavily, which is its well-known weakness. A non-linear fit to the same data is more reliable.

  • Km is an operational constant: it changes with pH, temperature and the second substrate.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Using substrate concentrations in different units on one line.
  • Including points where the rate has already plateaued.
  • Reading Km off the y-intercept instead of the x-intercept (which is −1/Km).

faq.q: What does a high Km mean?
faq.a: Low affinity: more substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax.

faq.q: How many points do I need?
faq.a: At least four, spread geometrically from about 0.2 to 5 × Km.

faq.q: What does the Lineweaver-Burk Plot / Km & Vmax actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns vmax, km and vmax/Km. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
